name: Shaka
info: Shaka kaSenzangakhona (c. 1787 – 1828) was king of the Zulu Kingdom from 1816 to 1828, remembered for reorganising the Zulu army and for wars whose part in the Mfecane remains disputed.

facts.born: July 1787 (the lunar month of uNtulikazi) at Mthonjaneni, in present-day KwaZulu-Natal; son of the Zulu king Senzangakhona kaJama and Nandi, spurned as illegitimate
facts.died: 24 September 1828, assassinated by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana with the iNduna Mbopa; his body was left in an empty grain pit
facts.role: Warrior and regiment commander under Dingiswayo of the Mthethwa; king of the Zulu Kingdom, 1816–1828
facts.known: Reorganising the Zulu army; the iklwa stabbing spear; the "bull horn" formation; the age-grade regiments; wars against Zwide of the Ndwandwe; the disputed role in the Mfecane

t: Shaka turned the Zulu from a small regional chiefdom into the leading power of southern Africa, ruling over 250,000 people and able to muster more than 50,000 warriors by his death in 1828.

He is credited with the iklwa stabbing spear, the "bull horn" formation and the age-grade regiments, though scholars dispute how far these were his inventions and how far he drew on existing practice.

His reign brought a massive number of deaths and coincided with the Mfecane, and how far he was to blame, and how far his image as a monster was made by European traders and later historians, is still argued.
dyk: Shaka's name is roughly translated as "intestinal beetle".
ev: Shaka is born at Mthonjaneni, son of the Zulu king Senzangakhona kaJama
Shaka becomes king of the Zulu
Shaka defeats Zwide's Ndwandwe at Gqokli Hill and on the Mhlatuze River and destroys Zwide's royal kraal
Shaka contends again with Zwide's son Sikhunyane
His mother Nandi dies; Shaka's mourning decrees bring mass executions
Shaka is assassinated by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana, and Dingane takes power

sections.early:
Shaka kaSenzangakhona was born in the lunar month of uNtulikazi (July) in 1787, at Mthonjaneni in present-day KwaZulu-Natal. He was the son of the reigning Zulu king, Senzangakhona kaJama, and the eldest of many sons, but he was regarded as illegitimate and sent away to live with his mother Nandi's people, the Elangeni, while a half-brother was left to rule. The Zulu of the time were a regional people living on livestock, sorghum and milk.

When he was old enough, Shaka and his mother were sent to the Mthethwa, the most powerful people of the region. There he grew up and was initiated into an ibutho lempi, a fighting regiment, serving as a warrior under Jobe and then under Dingiswayo, the respected chief of the Mthethwa. When Dingiswayo learned that Shaka was of royal birth he put him in charge of a regiment, which helped him develop his tactics and strategy. By this time Shaka was known for using the short stabbing spear, the iklwa. Sources tend to agree that he was tall and strongly built; his enemies called him ugly in some respects, and many said that he spoke with a speech impediment.
sections.rise:
Shaka became king of the Zulu in 1816 and refined the ibutho military system over the following years with the support of the Mthethwa Paramountcy, whom he still recognised as overlord. In his first years he had neither the influence nor the reputation to make any but the smallest groups join him. He forged alliances with smaller neighbours against raids by the Ndwandwe from the north, the most aggressive power of the region, and the Zulu's early moves were mainly defensive; he preferred to apply pressure through diplomacy, with an occasional strategic assassination.

Some years later Dingiswayo was ambushed and killed by Zwide's Ndwandwe; there is no evidence that Shaka betrayed him. Shaka then moved south across the Thukela River and set up his capital, Bulawayo, in Qwabe territory, where he may have intervened in a succession dispute to bring his own choice, Nqetho, to power. With the support of the Qwabe, Hlubi and Mkhize he was at last able to raise a force that could resist the Ndwandwe, and he won over friendly chiefs such as Zihlandlo of the Mkhize, Jobe of the Sithole and Mathubane of the Thuli through patronage and reward rather than battle.
sections.deeds:
Shaka's first major battle against Zwide was at Gqokli Hill on the Mfolozi River, where his troops held the crest against a frontal assault and his reserves swept round the hill to strike the enemy's rear. Losses were high, but the new methods were proven. In a two-day running battle on the Mhlatuze River the Zulu defeated the Ndwandwe, and Shaka led a fresh reserve some 110 kilometres to Zwide's royal kraal and destroyed it. Zwide escaped, and his general Soshangane moved north towards present-day Mozambique.

Shaka is credited with introducing the iklwa, a short stabbing spear with a broad blade, though he likely did not invent it; Zulu scholar John Laband says the training with it gave his warriors a "terrifying advantage". He is also thought to have introduced a larger shield, owned by the king and coloured by regiment. He organised the age grades into regiments quartered in military kraals, and most historians credit him with the "bull horn" formation, in which the veteran "chest" pinned the enemy, the young "horns" encircled it and the "loins" waited in reserve. Boys of six and over served as carriers. At his death he ruled over 250,000 people and could muster more than 50,000 warriors.
sections.opponents:
Shaka's chief enemy was Zwide, king of the Ndwandwe, who had killed Dingiswayo. Shaka is said to have killed Zwide's mother, Ntombazi, a sangoma, by locking her in a house with jackals or hyenas and burning it afterwards. His discipline was brutal: men who refused to go without sandals were killed, and according to the account H. Rider Haggard had from the later king Cetshwayo, a warrior who hesitated was executed after the fight and the wives and children of a defeated regiment were beaten to death. Laband dismisses the stories of sandals and of marches of 80 kilometres a day as myth, though other historians affirm that pace.

Historians are divided over Shaka himself. Some older histories denied his innovations or credited them to Europeans; some scholars hold that he was a borrower of methods and ruler-lineages already in place, citing J.H. Soga and A.T. Bryant on the short Zulu line beside the long pedigrees of the Hlubi, Ndwandwe and Swazi. The earliest accounts, by the traders Nathaniel Isaacs and Henry Francis Fynn, drew him as a pathological monster; Dan Wylie quotes Isaacs urging Fynn to make him "as bloodthirsty as you can", and Carolyn Hamilton argues that his image has been "invented" to suit later agendas.
sections.last:
Shaka's last year followed the death of his mother, Nandi, in October 1827. According to Donald Morris, he ordered that no crops be planted in the year of mourning, that no milk be used, and that any woman who became pregnant be killed with her husband; at least 7,000 people thought insufficiently grief-stricken were executed. Oral sources tell that a man named Gala finally objected that Nandi was not the first person to die in Zululand, and that Shaka called off the edicts and rewarded him with cattle.

His half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana appear to have tried at least twice to kill him, with support from Mpondo elements and some disaffected iziYendane. In 1828, most often dated to September, when nearly all the Zulu fighting men had been sent on a sweep to the north, the iNduna Mbopa created a diversion and Dingane and Mhlangana struck the fatal blows. Shaka's body was dumped in an empty grain pit filled with stones and mud; Morris holds that the site lies on Couper Street in KwaDukuza. Dingane took power and purged Shaka's supporters over several years.
sections.legacy:
Shaka's reign coincided with the start of the Mfecane or Difaqane, the devastating warfare and migrations in southern Africa between 1815 and 1840 that depopulated the region. Peoples fled out of reach of his impis, and his general Mzilikazi broke away to found the Ndebele state in present-day Zimbabwe; Soshangane and Zwangendaba also rose from the upheaval. Estimates of the Mfecane's dead usually range from 1 million to 2 million, but they are controversial, and some scholars warn that the theory neglects European encroachment and the slave trade. Julian Cobbing argues that the view of Shaka as the monster behind it served apartheid-era historians; others answer that the accounts of hundreds of victims and refugees, and sites such as the underground village of Lepalong, show the violence was real.

Military historians have compared his spear and formation to the Roman legion, and John Keegan, while noting myths, calls him "the greatest commander to have come out of Africa". In Zulu tradition he remains ambiguous, revered in praise songs and criticised in oral history. King Shaka International Airport near Durban, opened in 2010, bears his name.

summary: Shaka kaSenzangakhona ruled the Zulu Kingdom from 1816 to 1828, defeating Zwide's Ndwandwe and building an army of regiments armed with the stabbing spear. His rule brought many deaths and harsh discipline, and his part in the Mfecane is still disputed; he was assassinated by his half-brothers in 1828.

notes: The article's lead says 24 September 1828; its Death section says 'sometime in 1828; September is the most frequently cited date'. endCirca kept false, following the lead's exact date.
Birth: the lead says c. 1787 and also 'born in the lunar month of uNtulikazi (July) in 1787'; circa set true.

The article gives no year for Gqokli Hill or the Mhlatuze; it says Shaka and Zwide met near Pongola 'around 1825' and elsewhere that Zwide died in 1822, which contradict each other. I used '1820s' for the battles and left out the Pongola date.
The Ntombazi story is told in the article without attribution; hedged as 'is said to have'.
